subject: Business Models
title: Cable TV Bundles
description: A short lesson to help you apply Cable TV Bundles.

hook.text: You wanted ESPN but paid for 200 channels you never watched. That's bundling.

buildup.text: Cable companies bundled popular and niche channels together, forcing customers to buy the whole package.

discovery.text: Bundling works because it captures more consumer surplus. Each person values different channels highly.

twist.text: Streaming 'unbundled' cable—then rebundled: Disney+, Hulu, ESPN+ cost more together than cable did.

climax.text: Unbundling and rebundling is a cycle. Industries unbundle for disruption, then rebundle for profit.

punchline.text: Cut the cord, then subscribe to five apps. Bundles always return.

quiz.question: Why does bundling capture more consumer surplus?

details.summary: Cable TV bundling forced consumers to buy packages of hundreds of channels to access the few they actually watched, generating massive revenue per subscriber. This model maximized distributor and content creator income but ultimately drove cord-cutting as streaming offered cheaper alternatives.
details.whyItMatters: Cable bundling is a cautionary tale about extractive pricing. It generated enormous revenue for decades but created the customer resentment that fueled the streaming revolution..
takeaways: Consumers paid for hundreds of channels to access the few they wanted
Bundling maximized total industry revenue across content creators
Customer resentment of forced bundling accelerated streaming adoption

faq.question: Why was cable TV bundling so profitable for the industry?
faq.answer: Each niche channel added cents to the bundle cost but reached millions of subscribers who would never have paid individually. ESPN alone costs $9 per subscriber per month within the bundle. The aggregate bundle price exceeded what most consumers would pay for channels individually.

faq.question: Why did cable TV bundling eventually fail?
faq.answer: Streaming services offered specific content at lower prices without unwanted channels. Average cable bills exceeded $100 monthly. Younger consumers never developed cable habits. Internet speeds enabled streaming quality that matched cable. Annual price increases compounded customer frustration.
